basis: Noah’s preaching and the hearers saved
note: Clement presents Noah as preaching repentance and says those who heeded were saved; this early Christian retelling makes the outcome of a received admonition explicit.

basis: Clement’s Jonah as a model of heeded warning
note: Clement recalls that Jonah preached destruction to Nineveh and that the city repented and obtained pardon; this early Christian retelling reads the scriptural warning as a summons whose reception changes the announced outcome.

basis: The soils as different kinds of hearers
note: Chrysostom’s homily on the sower reads the soils as differing hearers of the word; this Christian interpretation develops why one proclamation bears fruit in some and not in others, much like the commentary’s two responses to reminder.

basis: One proclamation, opposed receptions
note: Paul says the word of the cross is foolishness to those perishing but God’s power to those being saved; one proclamation divides hearers by reception and outcome, like the commentary’s two responses.

basis: one message, perishing and saving hearers
note: The word of the cross is foolishness to those perishing and God's power to those being saved. Its divided audience gives a Christian message-and-recipient pattern, though its proclamation is not identical with the Qur'anic reminder.

basis: God as giver of growth beyond the teacher
note: Neither planter nor waterer is decisive, but God who gives growth. This reframes the commentary's reminder-giver limit through the Christian image of teachers who act without controlling the result.

basis: Timothy sent to remind communities
note: Paul sends Timothy to remind the Corinthians of Paul's ways in Christ, giving a mediated New Testament instance of a reminder passed from one person to another.

basis: mutual abstinence for prayer
note: Paul permits spouses temporary, agreed abstinence in order to devote themselves to prayer. This is a close Christian prayer-and-sexuality parallel, but frames abstention as voluntary and temporary rather than an automatic ritual bar.

basis: Knowing God and hearing his messengers
note: John says whoever knows God listens to the apostolic witnesses, while one not from God does not listen; this directly ties knowledge to receptivity, complementing the commentary’s discussion of knowledge and fear.

basis: receiving apostolic speech as God's word
note: The Thessalonians receive the word heard from messengers as God's word, which works in believers; it gives a concrete positive response to a delivered message.

basis: teaching that saves teacher and hearers
note: Persistent attention to life and teaching is said to save both the teacher and those who hear, making the possible benefit of instruction explicitly bilateral.

basis: The message among those saved and perishing
note: Paul calls the apostolic mission Christ’s fragrance among both those being saved and those perishing; the shared proclamation reaches audiences whose outcomes differ, adding a Christian account of divided reception.

basis: A fragrance from death or from life
note: Paul specifies that the same fragrance is for one person from death to death and for another from life to life; this sharpens the commentary’s contrast between the person who receives the reminder and the one who avoids it.

basis: Failure to see as imposed blindness
note: Paul says the god of this age has blinded unbelievers’ minds so they cannot see the gospel’s light; this gives a different account of failed reception from the commentary’s active image of the wretched person avoiding the reminder.

basis: intentional reminder to those who already know
note: The author intends continually to remind hearers of things they already know and in which they stand established; it directly supports the commentary's definition of reminder as a deliberate act toward others.

basis: gentle correction, repentance, knowledge
note: The teacher corrects opponents with gentleness in hope that God grants repentance leading to knowledge of truth; this closely accompanies the commentary's gentle address to Pharaoh and its fear-knowledge nexus.

basis: Scripture profitable for teaching and reproof
note: Scripture is called profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training, giving a direct Christian formulation of the reminder's possible usefulness.

basis: The preacher’s duty to reprove and exhort
note: Timothy is charged to proclaim the word and to reprove, rebuke, and exhort with patience; this gives a concrete Christian formulation of the admonisher’s task even when response varies.

basis: preaching, reproof, rebuke, and exhortation
note: The charge to proclaim the word includes reproof, rebuke, and exhortation with patient teaching, a direct Christian description of the outward act the commentary calls reminder.

basis: A hearer who will not endure sound teaching
note: Paul says people will not endure sound teaching and will gather teachers to suit their desires; this describes avoidance as actively selecting away from admonition.

basis: Turning the ears from truth
note: Paul says they will turn their ears away from truth and toward myths; the bodily image of turning away closely specifies the commentary’s image of keeping the reminder at a distance.

basis: turning hearing away from truth
note: Those described turn their hearing away from the truth and turn aside to myths, a verbal and spatially shaped counterpart to the recipient who avoids the reminder.

basis: Paul says his hearers thrust aside the word
note: Paul and Barnabas say their audience judged itself unworthy of eternal life by thrusting aside God’s word, so they turn to the Gentiles; this concretely depicts a hearer’s active rejection of the announcement.

basis: rejecting God's word and its consequence
note: Paul tells his audience that, by thrusting aside God's word, they judge themselves unworthy of eternal life. This is a missionary scene in which refusal of the offered word has a declared result.

basis: Gentile hearers rejoice and believe
note: The Gentiles rejoice when they hear Paul’s message and believe; this supplies the receptive counterpart in the same proclamation scene.

basis: Mockery and postponement after Paul’s announcement
note: In Athens, some mock when Paul speaks of resurrection, while others say they will hear him again; the scene records distinct responses to a public religious summons.

basis: Some hearers join and believe
note: The following verse names people who join Paul and believe; it completes the same scene with the response of hearers who accept the proclamation.

basis: Different responses to Paul’s explanation
note: After Paul explains the kingdom of God and argues from Moses and the prophets, some are persuaded and others disbelieve; this is a clear scene of one teaching meeting divided responses.

basis: Isaiah’s hard-hearing prophecy applied to Paul’s audience
note: Paul quotes Isaiah’s dull ears and closed eyes to explain why some hearers will not understand, turn, and be healed; this Christian continuation shows an interpretive tradition applying Isaiah’s account of failed reception to a new audience.

basis: Resisting the Spirit as the ancestors did
note: Stephen accuses his hearers of always resisting the Holy Spirit, as their ancestors did; this gives rejection of divine speech a repeated communal history.

basis: teaching and admonishing one another
note: The indwelling word leads the community to teach and admonish one another in wisdom, preserving the commentary's specifically interpersonal account of reminder.

basis: Do not refuse the one speaking
note: Hebrews warns its readers not to refuse the one speaking from heaven and recalls that those who refused the earthly warning did not escape; it explicitly joins refusal of admonition with judgment.

basis: refusing the one who speaks
note: The warning not to refuse the one who speaks preserves the commentary's agency distinction: a divine word is offered, and refusal is the hearer's perilous response.

basis: Pay closer attention lest hearers drift away
note: Hebrews urges readers to pay closer attention to what they heard so they do not drift away from it; this makes avoidance a gradual slipping from an already heard warning.

basis: attention to what was heard and drifting away
note: Hebrews calls for closer attention to what has been heard lest hearers drift away; the nautical image supplies a concrete Christian counterpart to turning aside from a reminder.

basis: Neglecting salvation has no escape
note: Hebrews asks how anyone can escape if they neglect such a great salvation; this adds the consequence of letting a saving announcement pass by.

basis: Daily exhortation against a hardened heart
note: Hebrews tells the community to exhort one another every day so no one is hardened by sin’s deceit; admonition is a mutual practice meant to keep hearers receptive.

basis: exhort one another against hardening
note: The community is to exhort one another daily so that none is hardened by sin's deceit; it makes repeated mutual reminder the antidote to the inward condition that refuses a divine word.

basis: Hearing without hardening
note: Hebrews repeats, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts”; this directly joins hearing a divine summons to the choice between receiving it and resisting it.

basis: The message that did not benefit its hearers
note: Hebrews says the good news heard by the wilderness generation did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith; this closely parallels the commentary’s question of whether the reminder benefits and makes faith the interpretive bridge.

basis: word heard but not beneficial
note: Hebrews says the word heard did not benefit its earlier hearers because it was not joined with faith, an unusually exact New Testament articulation of the commentary's conditional benefit of reminder.

basis: Receive the implanted word that can save
note: James tells readers to put away wickedness and receive meekly the implanted word, which can save their souls; this makes admonition a saving gift that must be welcomed.

basis: receiving the implanted word
note: James commands hearers to receive the implanted word, which is able to save them; its reception-versus-rejection logic makes the benefit of a delivered word explicit.

basis: Doers rather than hearers only
note: James warns readers not to be hearers only who deceive themselves, but to do the word; this distinguishes exposure to instruction from receiving it in practice.

basis: Doing the heard word brings blessing
note: James describes the person who looks into the law and perseveres as a doer who will be blessed in doing; it specifies the benefit of receiving instruction as practice, not mere hearing.

basis: Bringing a wanderer back from error
note: James says whoever brings a person wandering from truth back saves that person from death and covers many sins; this gives the reminder a neighbor-directed, restorative action.

basis: one person bringing back a wanderer
note: James imagines a person wandering from truth and another bringing that person back, an interpersonal counterpart to reminder aimed at someone who has moved away.

basis: turning a sinner back from wandering
note: The one who turns a sinner from wandering saves a soul from death and covers sins, making the benefit of successful corrective return concrete.

basis: Rejected words become the judge
note: Jesus says the one who rejects him and does not receive his words has a judge: the word he spoke will judge on the last day; it connects non-reception to the judgment that follows.

basis: evil-doer avoiding the light
note: The evil-doer hates the light and does not come to it lest deeds be exposed. Its avoidance is more active than verbal contradiction, clarifying the commentary's spatial account of shunning admonition.

basis: Hearing and believing lead from death to life
note: Jesus says the one who hears his word and believes the Father has eternal life and has passed from death to life; the verse links reception to a changed fate.

basis: Refusing to come for life
note: Jesus tells his interlocutors that they are unwilling to come to him to have life; this is a direct instance of refusing the offered source of life.

basis: hearing or rejecting the commissioned messenger
note: Jesus says that hearing his envoys is hearing him, while rejecting them reaches through to the sender. It clarifies the commentary's distinction between the reminder-giver and the addressee responsible for reception.

basis: Blessing belongs to those who keep the word
note: Jesus says blessed are those who hear God’s word and keep it; this pairs reception with obedience and the blessed outcome that contrasts with the commentary’s unhappy avoider.

basis: blessed hearers and keepers of God's word
note: Jesus calls those who hear God's word and keep it blessed, supplying the positive happy pole beside the commentary's fearful receiver and its contrast with the most wretched.

basis: Refusal of Moses and the Prophets
note: In the rich man’s story, Abraham says that those who do not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead; the warning cannot be made effective by a more spectacular sign when prior admonition is refused.

basis: The word held fast and made fruitful
note: Jesus says good-soil hearers hold the word fast in an honest and good heart and bear fruit with patience; this specifies an enduring form of the beneficial reception described in the commentary.

basis: Take care how you hear
note: Jesus warns his hearers to consider how they hear, since the one who has will receive more and the one who lacks will lose even what he thinks he has; this makes the consequences of response explicit.

basis: Jesus stops for a blind petitioner
note: Jesus stops and has the blind Bartimaeus called to him. Beside the commentary's rebuke of a prophet who turned from a blind seeker, it offers a controlled comparison of a religious teacher's response to a blind petitioner, not the same story.

basis: Joyful reception that does not last
note: In the sower parable, rocky-ground hearers receive the word at once with joy but fall away when trouble comes; this preserves a secondary case beyond simple acceptance or avoidance, where initial reception fails to endure.

basis: Hearing, accepting, and bearing fruit
note: In the sower parable, good soil represents those who hear the word, accept it, and bear fruit; this supplies a specific picture of a reminder that benefits its hearer.

basis: hearing, accepting, and bearing fruit
note: The good-soil hearers hear the word, accept it, and bear fruit; this gives a concrete Gospel image for a reminder whose reception has beneficial effect.

basis: nonreception of messenger and words
note: Where people neither receive the envoy nor hear the words, disciples leave and shake dust from their feet. It supplies a narrative counterpart to the commentary's limited role for the admonisher.

basis: Closed ears and an unhealed hearer
note: Matthew’s quotation of Isaiah describes a people whose heart has grown dull and ears are hard, so they do not hear, understand, turn, and receive healing; it gives a scriptural account of refusal as blocked reception.

basis: Disciples blessed with seeing and hearing
note: Jesus tells his disciples their eyes and ears are blessed because they see and hear; this supplies the positive counterpart to the dull hearing in the preceding verse and to the commentary’s fear-led recipient.

basis: correction and "if he hears you"
note: Private reproof is directed to a brother, and hearing the reprover gains that brother; it concretely pairs transitive admonition with a beneficial response.

basis: Jerusalem is unwilling to be gathered
note: Jesus says he often wanted to gather Jerusalem’s children as a hen gathers her brood, but they were unwilling; the image makes refusal of a protective summons concrete.

basis: Hearing and doing the sayings of Jesus
note: Jesus compares the one who hears his words and does them to a house built on rock; it gives a concrete outcome for receiving instruction rather than merely encountering it.

basis: hearing Jesus' words and doing them
note: The hearer who acts on Jesus' words is the wise house-builder; this gives an enacted Christian counterpart to beneficial reception of admonition.

basis: Hearing without doing
note: Jesus contrasts the person who hears his words but does not do them with the wise builder; the foolish house’s collapse makes the consequence of non-reception concrete.

basis: hearing without doing
note: The person who hears Jesus' words but does not act is the foolish house-builder, a distinct outcome for external hearing without the response commended in the commentary.

basis: Reproof as loving discipline
note: The risen Christ says he reproves and disciplines those he loves, then urges repentance; this Christian text interprets correction as care and gives the admonition a restorative purpose.

basis: God’s outstretched hands to a disobedient people
note: Paul quotes God’s all-day outstretched hands toward a disobedient and contrary people; the image pairs persistent invitation with refusal and gives a Christian rereading of Israel’s resistance to divine speech.

basis: first and second warning to a divisive person
note: After a first and second warning, the community is to decline further association with a divisive person. It gives a concrete Christian boundary for correction after a recipient proves unreceptive.

basis: responsibility to protest wrongdoing
note: The Bavli holds a person accountable for failing to protest wrongdoing within the reach of that person's influence. It is a Jewish extension of the duty to address another, complementing but not collapsing the commentary's limit on the reminder-giver.

basis: admonition that will be heeded
note: The Bavli's maxim that one should say a matter that will be heard and should not say one that will not be heard is a direct Jewish interpretive counterpart to the conditional "if the reminder benefits."

basis: Fearers reinterpreted as paired Torah learners
note: The Mishnah reads Malachi’s people who fear God and speak together as two who sit with words of Torah between them, with the divine presence among them; this rabbinic interpretation turns fearful reception into shared study, echoing the commentary’s description of admonition as passing to another.

basis: baal qeri and recitation of Shema
note: The mishnah limits a man with a seminal emission to inward reflection on the Shema rather than its normal verbal recitation. It provides a Jewish liturgical analogue to the commentary's association of the postcoital state with distance from prayer, without equating their rules.

basis: Fear as wisdom’s beginning
note: Ben Sira says fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; alongside the commentary’s account of fear as reverent and associated with knowledge, this Jewish wisdom text makes fear the entry into wisdom rather than its result.

basis: Those who fear the Lord do not disobey his words
note: Ben Sira says those who fear the Lord will not disobey his words and those who love him keep his ways; this directly links reverent fear with receiving and following instruction.

basis: Listening yields knowledge
note: Ben Sira says the one who loves listening gains knowledge and the attentive person becomes wise; this gives a concise account of instruction benefiting a receptive hearer.

basis: Fear expressed by hearing and serving
note: Samuel tells Israel that if they fear YHWH, serve him, and listen to his voice rather than rebel, they and their king will fare well; it directly links fear to taking divine instruction.

basis: Refusal brings the Lord’s hand against them
note: Samuel warns that if Israel will not listen to YHWH’s voice and rebels against his command, the Lord’s hand will be against them; this gives the non-hearing side its consequence.

basis: Obedience is better than sacrifice
note: Samuel tells Saul that listening to YHWH’s voice is better than sacrifice; the rebuke makes heedful response itself the required offering, not a religious substitute for it.

basis: Rejecting the word brings rejection
note: Samuel says Saul rejected YHWH’s word, so YHWH rejected him as king; this states the consequence of a ruler who hears the divine command but will not receive it.

basis: Despising words until judgment
note: The chronicler says the people mocked God’s messengers, despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets until wrath came; it is a concentrated account of rejecting repeated admonition and its outcome.

basis: Josiah hears the book and tears his clothes
note: When the king hears the words of the book of the law, he tears his clothes; the scene offers a concrete example of a hearer registering a warning rather than passing it by.

basis: A humbled response to heard words
note: Huldah says Josiah’s heart was tender and he humbled himself when he heard the words against Jerusalem, so God heard him; this makes inward responsiveness and its consequence explicit.

basis: Nocturnal emission and exclusion from camp
note: The commentary’s Arabic source note links junub with distance from prayer and the mosque; Deuteronomy orders a man with a nocturnal emission outside the camp until evening, a specific ritual-distance comparison, though its setting is the military camp and it says nothing about prayer.

basis: Washing and return at evening
note: Deuteronomy continues that the man washes and returns to camp at sunset; this clarifies the temporary boundary behind the commentary’s junub association while differing from its prayer-and-mosque framing.

basis: Choosing life rather than death
note: Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life; this gives a specific choice-and-consequence frame alongside the commentary’s contrast between the wretched and the opposite of happiness.

basis: public Torah reading, hearing, fear, observance
note: The commanded assembly is to hear, learn, fear YHWH, and observe Torah; its ordered response closely matches instruction received by one who fears.

basis: Hearing in order to learn fear
note: Moses recalls the assembly at Horeb so Israel would hear God’s words and learn to fear him throughout life, then teach their children; hearing instruction is explicitly the path to the reverent fear the commentary associates with receiving the reminder.

basis: assembled hearing, learning, fear, teaching
note: At Horeb the people are gathered to hear God's words, learn to fear him, and teach their children, giving a communal scriptural form to the commentary's reminder that passes from speaker to hearer.

basis: Hearing, fear, obedience, and well-being
note: After Israel hears God’s voice at Horeb, YHWH wishes they would keep a heart to fear him and his commands always, so it would go well with them and their children; this directly joins heard instruction, reverent fear, and benefit.

basis: heart that fears and obedience for good
note: YHWH wishes Israel had a heart to fear him and keep his commands so that it would go well with them; this joins reverential fear, reception of instruction, and benefit in one appeal.

basis: Arabic ذ ك ر and Hebrew זכר
note: The commentary labels the Arabic source root ذ ك ر and frames dhikrā as admonition; Hebrew זכר (zakar, “remember”) is cognate, and Moses uses it to command Israel to remember the wilderness road as a lesson in humility and keeping the commandments. The connection is the remembered lesson, not an equation of memory with admonition.

basis: Discipline understood as a father’s instruction
note: Moses tells Israel to know in its heart that YHWH disciplines it as a father disciplines a son; this offers a Jewish scriptural frame in which correction itself is instruction, though it does not describe the audience’s response to a spoken reminder.

basis: Moses confronts Pharaoh’s refusal
note: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh how long he will refuse to humble himself before YHWH and demand Israel’s release; this is the same ruler’s rejection of a divine summons, in the biblical narrative’s own terms.

basis: sexual abstention before theophany
note: Before Sinai's divine encounter the people are told not to approach a woman. It makes sexual abstention part of preparation for sacred approach, a related but not identical frame to the commentary's junub explanation.

basis: Arabic dhikr and Hebrew azkir
note: The Hiphil azkir, "cause my name to be remembered," belongs to the Hebrew zkr cognate family of Arabic dhikr. Its cultic setting adds an external, name-centred form of caused remembrance, not a claim that the two rituals are identical.

basis: Moses before Pharaoh; refusal to heed
note: In the Bible’s Moses–Pharaoh scene, Pharaoh asks who YHWH is and says he will not obey YHWH’s voice or release Israel; this gives the commentary’s rejected summons to Pharaoh a concrete counterpart, while making Pharaoh’s claimed ignorance explicit.

basis: Pharaoh's not knowing and not listening
note: Pharaoh answers Moses that he does not know YHWH and will not listen to his voice; it binds failed knowledge to refusal of the prophetic command, beside the commentary's offer of guidance intended to yield fear.

basis: Pharaoh’s servants fear YHWH’s word
note: The commentary says the one who fears takes the reminder; during the hail warning, Pharaoh’s servants who feared YHWH’s word hurried their servants and livestock to shelter, showing fear as heedful response.

basis: fear of YHWH's word and protective action
note: In the Moses-and-Pharaoh plague setting explicitly developed in the commentary, officials who fear YHWH's word act on the warning and bring servants and livestock under cover; reverent fear makes a transmitted warning beneficial.

basis: Failure to set the heart on the warning
note: The next verse says those who did not set their heart on YHWH’s word left their servants and livestock in the field; it gives a precise refusal alongside the fear-led response in the preceding verse.

basis: disregarding YHWH's word
note: The paired Pharaoh-scene verse describes the person who does not set his heart on YHWH's word and leaves those in his charge exposed, a concrete counterpart to the bedbaht recipient who keeps the reminder at a distance.

basis: harm to persons, animals, and crops in the field
note: The hail strikes people, animals, and vegetation left in the field, supplying the explicit harmful outcome beside the commentary's contrast between a warning that benefits and its disregard in the Pharaoh narrative.

basis: Turn so wrongdoing will not become ruin
note: Ezekiel urges Israel to repent and turn from its transgressions lest iniquity become its downfall; this makes the warning’s practical benefit explicit.

basis: Turn and live rather than die
note: YHWH says he takes no pleasure in anyone’s death and commands Israel to turn and live; this places a life-giving invitation beside the commentary’s contrast of the one who receives counsel and the wretched one who avoids it.

basis: Whether the rebellious hear or refuse
note: God tells Ezekiel that whether the rebellious house hears or refuses, its members will know a prophet has been among them; the message’s delivery is distinguished from its acceptance, as in the commentary’s divided audience.

basis: Speak the words whether heard or refused
note: Ezekiel is told to speak God’s words whether the rebellious hear or refuse; this clarifies the admonisher’s task even where the reminder may not benefit its audience.

basis: The warned wicked person who will not turn
note: The watchman is to warn the wicked; if the warned person does not turn, he dies in his iniquity while the watchman has delivered himself. This links offered warning, refusal, and consequence without making the messenger responsible for the hearer’s response.

basis: hear or refuse a prophetic word
note: Ezekiel is told to announce that whoever hears may hear and whoever refuses may refuse; the prophet delivers a word while the hearer divides into the two responses foregrounded here.

basis: God calls the wicked to turn from death
note: YHWH swears he takes no pleasure in the wicked person’s death but wants that person to turn and live, repeating “turn back”; it makes the offered warning’s life-preserving purpose unmistakable.

basis: Hearing without doing
note: The people come to Ezekiel, sit before him, and hear his words, yet do not do them; their mouths show love while their hearts pursue gain. This complicates a simple hear/refuse split by showing outward attendance without inward reception.

basis: hearing prophetic words without doing them
note: The audience sits before Ezekiel and hears his words but does not do them; it supplies the intermediate case the commentary's spatial account allows, outward proximity without inward reception.

basis: A prophet heard as a pleasant song
note: Ezekiel says his hearers treat his words like a beautiful song and listen without doing them; the image adds a form of non-reception in which people enjoy the sound of admonition while its claim passes them by.

basis: warning, turning, and the watchman's limit
note: If the watchman warns the wicked to turn, the warned person's response determines the outcome while the watchman has discharged his task; this illuminates both beneficial reminder and the commentary's limit on the reminder-giver.

basis: Arabic dhikr and Hebrew zkr/hizkir
note: Hebrew zkr is cognate with the source commentary's Arabic dhikr root. Joseph asks the cupbearer both to remember him and to cause Pharaoh to remember him, an especially clear instance of remembrance deliberately carried to another.

basis: Rejected knowledge and forgotten instruction
note: Hosea says the people are destroyed for lack of knowledge because they rejected knowledge and forgot God’s teaching; it connects the commentary’s knowledge-and-fear discussion to the consequence of refusing instruction.

basis: Willing obedience and good outcome
note: Isaiah says that if the people are willing and obedient they will eat the good of the land; it specifies a benefit for taking the prophetic demand to heart.

basis: willing obedience and good of the land
note: Willingness and obedience lead to eating the land's good, a concise prophetic rendering of the benefit pole in the commentary's benefit-and-harm contrast.

basis: Refusal and rebellion bring destruction
note: The paired warning says that if the people refuse and rebel, they will be devoured by the sword; it makes refusal of the same summons a concrete opposite outcome.

basis: refusal, rebellion, and devouring
note: The following alternative makes refusal and rebellion lead to being devoured by the sword, preserving the contrary harm pole in its own verse.

basis: a message of rest that hearers will not hear
note: The offered word identifies rest and relief for the weary, yet its hearers will not hear it; benefit is explicitly offered and then declined.

basis: Demanding smooth words from the prophets
note: The people tell seers not to see and prophets not to speak what is right, but to prophesy smooth things; this gives a specific way of avoiding correction by trying to control what the admonisher may say.

basis: request for smooth speech instead of what is right
note: The people tell seers not to see and prophets not to speak what is right, demanding smooth things and illusions. It specifies active evasion of admonition rather than a simple intellectual objection.

basis: Asking the Holy One to leave
note: They demand that the prophet turn aside from the way and that Israel’s Holy One cease from before them; this sharpens the commentary’s image of keeping the reminder at a distance into rejection of its divine source.

basis: A people unwilling to hear instruction
note: Isaiah calls them rebellious children who will not hear the instruction of YHWH; this directly names refusal of the teaching the commentary calls a reminder.

basis: teaching for benefit and leading in the way
note: YHWH describes himself as the one who teaches Israel for its benefit and leads it in the way it should go, joining the commentary's benefit of reminder to its secondary guidance language.

basis: The God-fearer listens to the servant’s voice
note: Isaiah asks who fears YHWH and obeys the voice of his servant, then tells that person to trust in YHWH while walking in darkness; this joins fear and listening while adding trust in a difficult circumstance.

basis: The word accomplishes its purpose
note: Isaiah compares God’s word to rain and snow that do not return without watering the earth, saying the word accomplishes God’s purpose; beside the commentary’s “if the reminder benefits,” this presents divine speech as effective, though not necessarily beneficial to every hearer.

basis: The wicked are urged to turn and receive pardon
note: Isaiah tells the wicked to forsake their way and return to YHWH, who will have compassion and abundantly pardon; this shows prophetic admonition offered for a hearer’s benefit, not only to announce judgment.

basis: Prophetic speech as judicial hardening
note: Isaiah’s commission continues by telling him to make the people’s heart dull and ears heavy, lest they turn and be healed; unlike the commentary’s account of the wretched person avoiding a reminder, this passage portrays non-reception within a judgment commission.

basis: Hearing without understanding in Isaiah’s commission
note: Isaiah is told to tell the people to hear without understanding and see without perceiving; in its own setting this is a prophetic commission to an unreceptive audience, offering a stark counter-scene to the commentary’s hearer who takes admonition.

basis: Trembling at God’s word
note: Isaiah says the Lord looks toward the lowly and contrite person who trembles at his word; this gives a scriptural profile for the commentary’s inwardly trembling hearer who receives admonition.

basis: trembling at God's word
note: Isaiah identifies the person who trembles at God's word; the bodily image and reverent reception give a close counterpart to the commentary's "içi titreyen" hearer.

basis: Those who tremble at the word amid hostility
note: Isaiah addresses hearers who tremble at YHWH’s word and then describes brothers who hate and expel them; this places reverent reception amid social hostility, a sharper conflict than the commentary’s brief contrast of receiver and avoider.

basis: fear that prevents turning away
note: God promises to put his fear in the people's hearts so that they will not turn away from him. It reverses the commentary's sequence by making fear the force that keeps a recipient from withdrawal.

basis: Officials fear after hearing the scroll
note: After Baruch reads Jeremiah’s words, the officials look at one another in fear and say they must report them to the king; the warning produces the kind of fear-led attention that the commentary associates with receiving counsel.

basis: The king burns the warning
note: As the scroll is read, Jehoiakim cuts off its columns and burns them; the act gives a stark, material form to the commentary’s image of the wretched keeping the reminder at a distance.

basis: The king and his servants feel no fear
note: The verse says the king and his servants were not afraid and did not tear their garments after hearing the words; it contrasts their response with the officials’ fear in 36:16 and shows refusal despite access to the warning.

basis: A warning intended to turn its hearers
note: Jeremiah’s scroll is to recount coming disaster so Judah may hear, turn from evil, and be forgiven; the passage makes the intended benefit of a reminder explicit.

basis: An offered way rejected by its hearers
note: Jeremiah urges people to seek the good ancient path and walk in it, but they answer that they will not; the scene makes rejection of offered guidance explicit.

basis: watchman's warning refused
note: When watchmen call for attention to the trumpet, the people answer that they will not listen. This is a direct prophetic-warning scene of the reminder being refused.

basis: Fear, wisdom, and turning from evil
note: Job’s poem identifies fear of the Lord with wisdom and turning from evil with understanding; this brings together the commentary’s knowledge-inflected fear and the distance from wrongdoing suggested by its avoidance language.

basis: fear of the Lord as wisdom
note: Job defines fear of the Lord as wisdom and departure from evil as understanding. It is a close Wisdom comparison to the commentary's fear-and-knowledge claim, while ordering the relation differently.

basis: Eliphaz calls the reproved person happy
note: Eliphaz says the person whom God reproves is happy and should not despise divine discipline; this touches the commentary’s contrast between the bedbaht and happiness, while remaining Eliphaz’s counsel within Job’s debate rather than an unqualified narrator verdict.

basis: God relents after seeing Nineveh’s response
note: The narrative says God saw that the Ninevites turned from their evil way and did not bring the announced disaster; this completes the warning’s benefit in the story with a changed outcome.

basis: Nineveh receives Jonah’s warning
note: After Jonah announces Nineveh’s overthrow, its people believe God, fast, and put on sackcloth; their response gives a narrative instance of warning being received and changing its hearers.

basis: blindness, ethical care, and fear of God
note: The prohibition against putting a stumbling block before the blind concludes with fear of God. It gives a Torah ethical setting for the commentary's blind, fearful visitor, though it is not the same incident.

basis: rebuke addressed to one's neighbour
note: The command to rebuke one's neighbour makes correction an act directed toward another person, matching the commentary's insistence that reminder is transitive rather than merely inward recollection.

basis: seminal emission and cultic exclusion
note: A priest affected by seminal emission may not eat holy things until clean. This supplies a Hebrew Bible ritual analogue to the commentary's postcoital distance claim, while the verse concerns holy food rather than mosque prayer.

basis: Those who fear speak to one another
note: Malachi describes those who fear YHWH speaking with one another while YHWH listens and records them; this turns the commentary’s fear-led reception into a communal exchange whose hearers are remembered by God.

basis: Arabic dhikrā and Hebrew זכרון
note: The commentary labels Arabic ذ ك ر as its source root and uses dhikrā for admonition; Malachi’s זכרון (zikaron, “remembrance”) uses the cognate Hebrew root for the record of those who fear YHWH and speak together, where the sense is memorial rather than instruction.

basis: fearers and a book of zikkaron
note: The verse couples those who fear YHWH with a written zikkaron, "remembrance," from the Hebrew cognate family of dhikr; it is a distinct divine memorial usage alongside the commentary's human-directed reminder.

basis: Wisdom calls and is refused
note: Personified Wisdom says she called and was refused and stretched out her hand without being heeded; this gives the bedbaht’s avoidance of offered admonition a specific scriptural scene.

basis: Rejected knowledge and unchosen fear
note: Wisdom’s opponents are said to hate knowledge and not choose fear of YHWH; alongside the commentary’s Arabic source note linking خشية to “I knew” and its claim that fear commonly arises from knowledge, Proverbs gives the relation in the opposite pedagogical direction.

basis: hating knowledge and not choosing fear
note: The rejected way is specified as both hatred of knowledge and refusal to choose the fear of YHWH, a precise negative counterpart to the fearful rememberer.

basis: The listener’s security
note: Wisdom says whoever listens will dwell securely and be at ease without dread of disaster; this adds safety as the outcome of attending to counsel, while the commentary emphasizes the receiver’s fear as the disposition that makes listening possible.

basis: fear as beginning of knowledge
note: Proverbs calls fear of YHWH the beginning of knowledge, whereas the commentary says its reverential fear commonly arises from knowledge. The differing order is the point of comparison, while both tightly link the two.

basis: Instruction as a path of life
note: Proverbs says the one who heeds instruction is on a path of life, while the one who rejects reproof leads others astray; it gives both the benefit of receiving counsel and the danger of refusing it.

basis: The son who hears versus the scoffer
note: A wise son hears his father’s instruction, while a scoffer does not listen to rebuke; this is another precise contrast between a teachable recipient and one who avoids admonition.

basis: soft answer that turns wrath
note: The gentle speech commanded to Moses and Aaron in the commentary has a Wisdom analogue in the soft answer that turns away wrath; both treat the manner of address as consequential.

basis: Listening to life-giving reproof
note: The one whose ear listens to life-giving reproof dwells among the wise; this closely matches the commentary’s hearer who receives admonition through an inwardly responsive disposition.

basis: an ear listening to life-giving reproof
note: The verse calls reproof "life-giving" and locates its effect in an ear that listens, an exact Wisdom formulation of a beneficial admonition received by its hearer.

basis: Ignoring instruction versus heeding reproof
note: Proverbs contrasts the person who ignores instruction and harms himself with the one who heeds reproof and gains understanding, spelling out both sides of the commentary’s reception/avoidance contrast.

basis: ignoring instruction versus listening to reproof
note: Ignoring discipline is self-despising, while listening to reproof gains understanding; this makes the two possible responses to instruction carry opposed effects.

basis: reproof penetrating the understanding person
note: A rebuke enters more deeply into one with understanding than repeated blows into a fool, distinguishing a receptive, knowing addressee from a resistant one.

basis: fear of YHWH and knowledge of God
note: This verse places understanding the fear of YHWH alongside finding knowledge of God, supplying a Wisdom counterpart to the commentary's close account of fear and knowledge.

basis: wise reprover and listening ear
note: The wise reprover is compared to precious adornment for a listening ear, a precise image of admonition whose value depends on a receptive recipient.

basis: A stiff neck after repeated reproof
note: The person often reproved who stiffens his neck will suddenly be broken beyond healing; this develops the fate of persistent refusal beyond the single act of avoiding a reminder.

basis: turn away and pass on from an evil path
note: The sage commands turning away and passing on from the path of the wicked. Its spatial idiom reverses the commentary's moral allocation: avoidance is wise when its object is evil, whereas its wretched recipient avoids beneficial reminder.

basis: Different responses to rebuke
note: Proverbs says rebuking a scoffer brings hatred but rebuking a wise person brings love; like the commentary’s contrast between the one who takes the reminder and the one who avoids it, the response depends on the hearer.

basis: reproof received by wise, hated by scoffer
note: The proverb differentiates the recipient of reproof: the scoffer hates correction while the wise person loves it, a compact analogue to reminder received by one person and avoided by another.

basis: Instruction increases the wise hearer’s learning
note: The verse says instruction makes the wise wiser and teaching increases the righteous person’s learning; it supplies a concrete account of how admonition benefits the receptive hearer.

basis: A blessed person refuses wicked counsel
note: The psalm calls blessed the person who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked; unlike the bedbaht who avoids divine admonition, this person’s distance is good because of what is refused, making the object of avoidance decisive.

basis: happiness and keeping away from wicked counsel
note: Psalm 1 calls happy the person who keeps away from wicked counsel. Its ethical allocation reverses the commentary's image: distance is good when the counsel is wicked, while keeping a beneficial reminder distant marks the wretched person.

basis: Fear as the beginning of wisdom
note: The psalm says fear of YHWH is the beginning of wisdom and that those who practice the commands have good understanding; it links fear and knowledge in the reverse direction from the commentary’s claim that fear commonly arises from knowledge.

basis: Warning and reward in keeping instruction
note: The psalm says God’s rules warn the servant and that keeping them brings great reward; this joins an admonition’s warning function to a concrete benefit, as the commentary asks whether the reminder benefits.

basis: The God-fearer is taught the way
note: The psalm asks who fears YHWH and answers that God will instruct that person in the way to choose; it reverses the commentary’s order in a useful way, making fear the disposition that receives instruction.

basis: teacher's address and fear of YHWH
note: "Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of YHWH" makes fear the explicit subject of a directed instruction, rather than an undifferentiated emotion.

basis: Casting instruction behind oneself
note: In God’s indictment of people who recite his statutes, the wicked are said to hate discipline and cast God’s words behind them; this makes rejection of instruction a deliberate act, close to the bedbaht’s avoidance.

basis: Refusal followed by one’s own counsel
note: After Israel would not listen to God’s voice, the psalm says he gave them over to their stubborn hearts to walk in their own counsel; this connects refusal of a divine reminder with self-directed wandering.

basis: The good outcome of listening
note: God says that if Israel would listen and walk in his ways, he would quickly subdue its enemies; the verse gives a concrete benefit that refusal has forfeited.

basis: The flock summoned to hear God’s voice
note: The psalm calls Israel the people of God’s pasture and the sheep of his hand, then says “today, if you hear his voice”; it frames reception of divine speech as the present duty of the addressed community.

basis: "today" and hearing God's voice
note: The Psalm's urgent "Today, if you hear his voice" casts receptivity to divine speech as a present decision, directly sharpening the commentary's offered reminder and its possible uptake.

basis: Do not harden the heart when hearing
note: The psalm warns its hearers not to harden their hearts as at Meribah; it makes the inner refusal that counters a receptive, trembling hearer explicit.

basis: hardening the heart against hearing
note: The command not to harden the heart gives a specific inner opposite to the fearful hearer: an inward state that converts hearing into resistance.

basis: Turning away and stopping the ears
note: Zechariah says the ancestors refused to pay attention, turned a stubborn shoulder, and stopped their ears; the bodily gestures make the commentary’s language of passing by an admonition concrete.

basis: turning the shoulder and stopping the ears
note: Those addressed refuse attention, turn a stubborn shoulder, and stop their ears from hearing; its physical language of withdrawal closely specifies the commentary's claim that the wretched person keeps admonition away rather than simply arguing with it.

basis: A hardened heart that will not hear
note: The people made their hearts hard lest they hear the Torah and the words sent through earlier prophets, bringing great wrath; the verse ties refusal of warning to a chosen incapacity to receive it.

basis: Sinai’s acceptance under threat and later reaffirmation
note: The Talmud imagines the mountain held over Israel as a barrel, with acceptance of Torah demanded under threat of burial, then says Israel reaffirmed acceptance in Ahasuerus’s days; this complicates a simple equation of reception with inward reverent fear by distinguishing coerced and later willing acceptance.
